title: Improper compression for Gaussian-mixture reconstruction
formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learning procedure with the following guarantee? For all integers \(d\ge1\), \(k>d\) and \(t\ge2\), and every Borel probability distribution \(D\) on the closed Euclidean unit ball \(B_d\), it learns a shared model \(w\) and an encoder–decoder pair \(E_w:B_d\to\{0,1\}^{b}\), \(Q_w:\{0,1\}^{b}\to B_d\) such that, with probability at least \(2/3\), \[\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\|Q_w(E_w(x))-x\|_2^{2}\le\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)+1/t,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(D)=\inf_{\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\in B_d}\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\min_{i\in[k]}\|x-\mu_i\|_2^{2}?\] Training, sample count, model storage, encoding and decoding must all be polynomial in \(d,k,t\), while the number of bits per encoded point satisfies \(b\le C(1+\log_2 k+\log_2 t)^{q}\) for universal \(C,q>0\). This is the explicitly normalized, bounded-data version of the source's first reconstruction question, in the overcomplete regime \(k>d\).
why: The task asks whether efficient unsupervised reconstruction can compete with a small optimal codebook while using only a polynomial in the logarithms of its size and accuracy per point. It separates the cost of discovering original mixture parameters from the cost of learning a useful compact representation.
status_note: The first reconstruction question is open in the COLT 2018 source. The bounded-data real-RAM version is an explicit editorial specification, not a verbatim complete model supplied there. Bounded searches on 2026-09-14 found later Gaussian-mixture compression results for density estimation, whose objective and time guarantees differ. No matching resolution was verified, and the search is not exhaustive.

Hazan and Livni ask for polynomial-in-logarithms encoding length and efficient improper reconstruction in the overcomplete regime. Their PCA comparison does not attain the requested pointwise encoding length.
Ashtiani and coauthors obtain near-optimal Gaussian-mixture density-estimation sample bounds through distribution compression, a different objective and resource guarantee.

importance.reason: Tests whether allowing a learned improper representation removes a computational obstruction while preserving a compact per-point code; the bounded reconstruction target is distinct from estimating mixture densities or parameters.
importance.basis: Saved question, title, and category scope; importance review only, not a fresh proof or open-status review.

sentences: The task is to learn short pointwise encodings that reconstruct bounded Euclidean data almost as well as the best k centers.
It concerns the overcomplete regime, where the number of comparator centers exceeds the ambient dimension.
The decoder may be improper and share a learned model, but each new point receives only polynomial-in-logarithms many bits.
The card explicitly fixes unit-ball normalization, squared reconstruction loss and polynomial real-arithmetic training and evaluation.
Density-estimation compression results use a different objective and do not by themselves settle this task.

definitions:
Here \(B_d=\{x\in\mathbb R^{d}:\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{2}\le1\}\), \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), and \(\|x\|_2^{2}=\sum_jx_j^{2}\). The comparator is the best set of \(k\) reconstruction centers; repeated centers are allowed. The distribution need not itself be a Gaussian mixture. There is no separation, covariance or minimum cluster-weight promise. Accuracy is additive squared Euclidean reconstruction error in these unit-ball coordinates. The integer \(t\) requests error \(1/t\); all positive accuracy levels are covered by rounding to a smaller reciprocal-integer tolerance.

Fix three finite programs, for training, encoding and decoding. They use a real RAM with rational program constants, exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square roots of nonnegative values, comparisons and indexed memory access, each charged one operation. Integer counters and addresses use logarithmically many bits in \(d+k+t+2\), with a fixed constant factor allowed for each program. There is no floor operation, real-digit extraction, advice, or noncomputable real program constant. Training also has independent fair random bits and a sampling oracle returning independent points from \(D\). One sample request and reading each of its coordinates are charged. There must be one polynomial \(p\), independent of \(D,d,k,t\), bounding training operations, samples, and stored scalar or integer cells, and bounding operations for encoding any one point and decoding any codeword. All executions must halt within these bounds, even on the probability-of-failure event.

Training returns a finite shared parameter vector \(w\) and the integer code length \(b\); the two fixed evaluation programs use \(w,d,k,t,b\). They are deterministic after training. Every codeword has exactly \(b\) bits, with padding allowed. The decoder receives only that codeword and the shared model, and returns a point in \(B_d\). The original point and extra point-dependent information are unavailable to it. Model storage is charged to the polynomial storage bound, not again to each point's code length. Probability of training success is over its samples and random bits; the expectation in the successful guarantee uses a fresh independent point. No restriction to a nearest-center decoder or to \(k\) possible reconstructions is imposed.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of the three uniform procedures and universal polynomial and code-length bounds, with the stated error guarantee, or a proof that no such procedures exist in this model. A negative result for a proper Gaussian-parameter estimator or a decoder restricted to exactly \(k\) centers does not refute this improper target. A multiplicative constant greater than one in front of \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)\) does not meet the required additive guarantee.

context_blocks.text: The Gaussian-mixture title motivates the comparator, but the source deliberately uses a non-generative reconstruction objective to permit improper learning. Recovering Gaussian densities or component parameters is a different task. A successful encoder and decoder need only achieve the specified squared-distance loss.

The 2018 note leaves normalization and the detailed computational model implicit. This card explicitly selects unit-ball data and real-arithmetic polynomial time, drawing on the normalized reconstruction framework it cites. This bounded-data target is not asserted equivalent to every distribution on unbounded Euclidean space. It retains the source’s first, spherical-comparator question; the additional general-covariance direction is not folded into it.

A nearest-center code for a known set of k centers needs only a logarithmic number of bits for the center index. The challenge includes learning from samples. The source’s linear-subspace comparison has a substantially larger pointwise representation when the number of retained coordinates is large.

The 2020 JACM paper proves sample-complexity bounds for approximating Gaussian-mixture densities in total variation, using compression of a distribution description. It explicitly does not optimize running time. Those results do not establish polynomial-time, short-code reconstruction of each new point in the model here.
